facts.statement: The only known species in the genus Megavitiornis is Megavitiornis altirostris.
The genus Megavitiornis was described by Trevor Worthy in the year 2000.
Fossils of Megavitiornis date to the Holocene epoch.
Megavitiornis altirostris was an extinct, flightless, giant bird endemic to Fiji.
facts.quote: Megavitiornis altirostris is an extinct, flightless, giant stem-galliform bird that was endemic to Fiji

facts.statement: Recent studies place Megavitiornis in the family Sylviornithidae, outside the Galliformes crown group, related to Sylviornis.
facts.quote: more recent morphological studies indicate a close relationship with Sylviornis of New Caledonia, with both genera belonging to the family Sylviornithidae outside of the Galliformes crown group

facts.statement: Researchers suggest Megavitiornis likely went extinct due to overhunting by humans after they colonized Fiji.
facts.quote: It is likely that it became extinct through overhunting shortly after the colonisation of the Fiji Islands by humans

facts.statement: The genus Megavitiornis is monotypic, containing only one species.
The species name altirostris refers to the bird's extraordinarily large vertical bill dimension.
facts.quote: The specific epithet altirostris comes from Latin altus (high or noble), and rostrum (bill), referring to the extraordinarily large vertical dimension of its bill

facts.statement: Trevor Worthy described Megavitiornis in October 1998.
facts.quote: It was described by New Zealand palaeontologist Trevor Worthy in October 1998

facts.statement: Remains of Megavitiornis have been found in caves on Viti Levu and Naigani Island.
facts.quote: Sites containing remains include the Udit Tomo cave at Wainibuku, Voli Voli and Delai-ni-qara caves on the island of Viti Levu, as well as on Naigani Island

facts.statement: Megavitiornis was likely the largest bird in Fiji during its time.
facts.quote: In its time it was probably the largest bird in Fiji

facts.statement: Megavitiornis showed signs of flightlessness through its large body size, reduced pectoral girdle, and lack of a sternum keel.
facts.quote: The bird's flightlessness is evident in its large body size, the extreme reduction of pectoral girdle elements and the loss of a keel on the sternum

facts.statement: The bill of Megavitiornis was extraordinarily deep, measuring 28% of its total length.
facts.quote: with a depth of 28% of the length, extraordinarily deep compared to modern galliforms

facts.statement: Trevor Worthy speculates that Megavitiornis used its bill to crack hard seeds of large forest fruits.
facts.quote: Worthy speculates that it was used for cracking the hard seeds of large forest fruits

facts.statement: The parent group of the genus Megavitiornis is Sylviornithidae.
Megavitiornis lived from the Late Pleistocene to the Holocene, between 0.129 and 0 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Late Pleistocene to Holocene (0.129 to 0 million years ago)

rejected.statement: Megavitiornis belongs to the class Aves.
